title: Leadership The Moment Before You Respond Kathleen Schafer
author: Schafer, Kathleen
summary: Between every stimulus and response exists a moment of choice — a brief pause that, when cultivated, can transform leadership. Most leaders learn through collision rather than by practicing the pause before the wreckage occurs. The central question in that moment is not 'how do I win?' but 'what do I want to create?' — connection, clarity, accountability. Opinion becomes destructive when it fuels reaction: wanting to be understood, we become louder; wanting respect, we become controlling. True leadership requires choosing peace not as defeat but as a wider space for truth. A community committed only to its own rightness is not a community but a collection of defended individuals, each armored, each alone. As the pause is practiced over time, small irritations lose authority and the need to dominate gives way to the desire to understand. Closes with Viktor Frankl: 'Between stimulus and response there is a space.'
points: In the moment before responding, leadership is available — the kind that shapes not just the conversation but the quality of everything being built together.

'Do you want to be right or happy?' — asks whether your deepest intention is dominance or peace, whether you want to stand above someone with the satisfaction of winning or stay in the room long enough for something shared to become possible.
A community of people committed only to their own rightness is not really a community — it is a collection of defended individuals, each certain, each armored, each alone.
Conscious choice sometimes means stopping the explanation, leaving the room, or naming that a conversation cannot continue as it is going — these are leadership acts, not retreats.
As the pause is practiced, little irritations lose their authority; the need to dominate gives way to the desire to understand.
quotes: There is a moment before we respond. Sometimes it is only a breath, sometimes so brief we miss it entirely. But in that moment, leadership is available, the kind that shapes not just the conversation in front of us but the quality of everything we are building together.

When opinion becomes the fuel for reaction, it moves us toward the very thing we say we do not want. We want to be understood, so we become louder. We want respect, so we become controlling. We want peace, so we disappear. We want honesty, so we become harsh.

It is not asking us to abandon truth or become falsely agreeable. It is asking whether our deepest intention is dominance or peace, whether we want to stand above the other person with the satisfaction of having won, or stay in the room long enough for something shared to become possible. Choosing peace doesn't diminish truth. It creates a wider space for truth to be heard.
Truth does not need to humiliate. Clarity does not require contempt. Strength does not need to overpower. And leadership is not proven by having the last word.
A community of people committed only to their own rightness is not really a community, it is a collection of defended individuals, each one certain, each one armored, each one alone.
Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose our response. In our response lies our growth and our freedom. — Viktor Frankl
